title: CEO Interview With Trey Closson of Amplio
gist: Amplio's CEO argues US manufacturers strand tens of billions of dollars in surplus equipment and spares because nobody owns surplus, and pitches an AI-driven, profit-share recovery service. Figures are founder-supplied and promotional, though the interest-rate carrying-cost point and semiconductor subfab angle are notable.

themes.theme: Size and cause of surplus waste

insights.claim: US manufacturers invest roughly $1.5 trillion a year in equipment and parts, a meaningful share of which never earns a return, with directly observable waste of $60 billion to $100 billion-plus a year.
insights.speaker: Trey Closson
insights.so_what: Founder-estimated addressable market for industrial asset recovery.
insights.quote: US manufacturers invest roughly $1.5 trillion a year in equipment and parts

insights.claim: MRO storerooms often hold 25 to 40 percent dormant inventory, and cancelled projects and facility closures create stranded equipment.
insights.speaker: Trey Closson
insights.so_what: Dormant inventory is large and recurring across plants.

insights.claim: The root cause of surplus is incentives, not ignorance: plant teams overstock to protect uptime, operations is measured on throughput, finance defers write-offs, and nobody owns surplus, so the default is abandonment.
insights.speaker: Trey Closson
insights.so_what: Misaligned internal incentives explain persistent inefficiency and create a services niche.
insights.quote: The root cause is incentives, not ignorance.

insights.claim: Fewer than 1 in 10 manufacturers have a dedicated investment recovery function, and a plant closure can take four to six separate vendors, with liquidators taking the best assets and leaving the rest.
insights.speaker: Trey Closson
insights.so_what: Fragmented recovery market with no dominant full-service provider.

insights.claim: A $30 million dormant MRO inventory looked tolerable at near-zero interest rates, but at 5 to 6 percent the wasted carrying costs bite much harder.
insights.speaker: Trey Closson
insights.so_what: Higher rates raise the cost of idle inventory and push working capital recovery up the priority list.
insights.quote: At 5 to 6 percent, wasted carrying costs bite much harder.
insights.locator: What keeps your customers up at night?

insights.claim: Amplio's biggest competitor is doing nothing, followed by cherry-picking liquidators, local dealers, auctions, large full-service firms and DIY listings, each of which serves only a slice.
insights.speaker: Trey Closson
insights.so_what: Inertia, not rivals, is the primary barrier for this category.
insights.quote: Our biggest competitor is doing nothing.
insights.locator: What does the competitive landscape look like

insights.claim: Auctions work for liquid categories like rolling stock but struggle with custom or thin-market parts, category specialists leave a still-stuffed storeroom, and full-service firms offer rigid buyouts focused on the top of the market.
insights.speaker: Trey Closson
insights.so_what: Maps each incumbent's gap, which defines Amplio's whole-site positioning.

insights.claim: Amplio claims clients see recovery up to 5x industry standards, and differentiates through free upfront valuation, whole-problem scope, AI pricing from secondary-market comparables with human review, and no upfront fees with profit share.
insights.speaker: Trey Closson
insights.so_what: Unverified headline claim; profit-share model aligns incentives.
insights.quote: Clients are seeing recovery up to 5x industry standards.

insights.claim: For semiconductor and electronics manufacturers the sweet spot is everything around the process tools: spare parts storerooms, subfab equipment such as pumps, chillers, valves, power and controls, plus test equipment and IT hardware.
insights.speaker: Trey Closson
insights.so_what: Fab spares and subfab equipment form a secondary market that surfaces during fab closures and retoolings.
insights.locator: Which asset categories and industries are your strongest?

themes.theme: AI and agentic orchestration in industrial services

insights.claim: Amplio is building agentic systems to run the surplus lifecycle end to end, from cataloging and appraisal to channel routing, invoicing and logistics, with humans stepping in only where strategic judgment matters.
insights.speaker: Trey Closson
insights.so_what: Agentic workflow replaces time-intensive handoffs in legacy liquidation services.

insights.claim: Amplio turns photos and documents into a usable catalog in minutes instead of days, and each completed deal feeds SKU-level outcome data back so each valuation sharpens the next.
insights.speaker: Trey Closson
insights.so_what: Proprietary transaction data creates a compounding pricing advantage.

insights.claim: Amplio closed an $11.1M Series A in September 2025 led by Hitachi Ventures and Yamaha Motor Ventures, with clients including Georgia-Pacific, General Motors, Anheuser-Busch and NCR Voyix.
insights.speaker: Trey Closson
insights.so_what: Shows early institutional and enterprise validation.
